posts.content:
A new product launch is no small thing, and neither is the sales training.

You know the usual drill. The product team walks the sales team through every button and every spec. Thorough and detailed. 

But too often, that's where it ends.

That's where marketing needs to explain the who and why behind the what and how. 

Knowing a product and knowing how to sell it are two different things.

We'll discuss all that and more on our next #IMCL webinar for B2B marketers at 10 a.m. CT this Thursday.

Stu Accola will be joining us to talk about how he's helped develop sales trainings that actually generate more sales.

He'll walk us through:
✅ Why a rep carrying 200 to 300 accounts can't push everything everywhere
✅ What belongs in a complete sales training, and what most launches skip
✅ How to earn the buy-in so the materials you built actually get used
✅ Why "I made all this stuff and nobody used it" keeps happening

Overall, messaging consistency is key. 

If a buyer hears one thing from a rep and reads something different on your website, that's always a problem.

Plus, if you don't feel marketing is involved enough in the product development and/or sales process, being involved in sales training is a great way to get yourself a seat at the table.

Just ask Stu!

Join the Collective for "Developing sales trainings that actually sell."

#B2BMarketing #industrialmarketing #IndustrialMarketingCollectiveLive
#salestraining

posts.content:
More than 50% of sales calls I conduct with B2B manufacturers are driven by their desire for "more leads now through search":

Google ads / SEO / AEO / GEO / LLMO / OtherKindsOfOs

But here's what many of them overlook:

On any given day, only 1-3% of the people whose attention they want are in the market looking to make a change. The other 97-99% aren't looking today, and most of them won't be for months (or longer).

Nobody wakes up on a Tuesday and decides to replace a $500K piece of equipment that's worked fine for fifteen years. Something has to trigger the change. A line goes down, a key supplier fumbles an order, a plant manager retires, a new regulation lands.

You don't get to decide when those triggers happen.

But you also can't just sit around waiting for them.

That's why the real marketing work is to start building trust and visibility with that 97-99% right NOW. That means today, next week, next month and all year long by showing up consistently with content that's genuinely useful to the right people, long before any of them are ready to buy.

Do that, and something powerful happens. When the trigger finally comes, you won't be just another search result getting compared to four others:

You'll be the company they already know and the one they already believe can help them. You'll also be the one the ChatGPTs and Geminis and Claudes start to recommend.

It takes patience. But it's the kind of patience most of your competitors won't have because all they're focused on is "more leads now".

posts.content:
There are two camps in the AI conversation right now.

Camp one: AI will replace every marketer. Camp two: AI only produces generic slop.

We at Gorilla 76 think both are wrong.

At Gorilla 76, we use AI because it's useful. Agencies that ignore it are leaving real value on the table. But it has to be used responsibly.

Here's how we actually think about it.

AI is good for what it's good at — brainstorming, outlining, summarizing, cleaning up transcripts, speeding up legwork. It helps you move faster and get past the blank page.

What it can't do is replace experienced people making smart decisions.

Our clients hire us for professional judgment, not an AI platform's. So if something goes out under our name or a client's, a human being is responsible for it. Everything gets carefully written, edited and fact-checked. Anything vague, incorrect or generic gets fixed or cut.

We've all seen what happens when people skip those steps.

A few things that haven't changed just because the tools have:

✅ Accuracy still matters. The fact that something can be generated quickly doesn't make it worth publishing.

✅ Confidentiality still matters. We're careful about what goes into these tools — sensitive client data never goes into an unsecured platform.

✅ Standards still matter. We're not interested in plagiarizing, misrepresenting or rushing through work just because the machine makes it easy.

AI may help us brainstorm or structure information. But it is not doing the thinking for us.

Clients don't hire agencies for the tools they subscribe to. They hire agencies for taste, expertise and perspective.

That's not changing.

👉 How is your team navigating AI in your marketing work? 

We'd love to hear where you've found it useful — and where you've hit walls.

#b2bmarketing #industrialmarketing #aimarketing #AI #AIO

Industrial marketers are under pressure to “use AI,”  but the real challenge isn’t adoption. It’s using it well.

On this week’s IMC Live, we’re sharing how our team approaches generative AI with strategy, ethics and practical structure. Not templates. Not shortcuts. A framework.

Here’s what we’ll unpack:

𝐖𝐡𝐲 “𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐞 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐞𝐥𝐬𝐞’𝐬 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰” 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭
Copy/paste AI usage limits your thinking and weakens your brand voice.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞-𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭, 𝐀𝐈-𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐤𝐞
Rooted in strategic principles, not novelty.

𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡-𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐨𝐧
 – 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘛𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘯𝘦𝘳: clarifying ideas, stress-testing assumptions
 – 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘋𝘦𝘵𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘦: researching, recognizing patterns, developing deeper insights
 – 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘌𝘹𝘦𝘤𝘶𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘳: turning strategy into clean, consistent output

Our goal: help industrial marketers develop their own effective use cases — ones aligned to their role, their goals and their way of thinking.

📆 Join us 12/4 at 10 a.m. CDT for IMC Live: How Gorilla 76 uses generative AI with intention.

posts.content:
Yesterday I had the honor of speaking at University of North Carolina Wilmington Business Week hosted by the Cameron School of Business at UNC Wilmington

My session was titled “Don’t Wait for Permission: How to Build a Marketing Career in 2026”

I opened my session by saying “I want to deliver the talk I wish I heard when I was in your shoes”

Because when I graduated in 2015 with an English degree and no real industry connections or career roadmap, I had to figure out a lot on my own.

So I shared the story of how I’ve built my marketing career and how anyone can do the same thing today.

I broke it down into 4 main ingredients:

1️⃣ Get out of theory and into building real, practical skills. 

2️⃣ Learn how to show the measurable results of your work. Real business outcomes.

3️⃣ Be adaptable. Pursue continuous curiosity and learning.

4️⃣ Build relationships. Work hard, say “hi” to strangers, make your work visible, and be kind.

I absolutely love opportunities like this to share what I’ve learned with the next wave of marketers so I’m very grateful to the folks who gave me the opportunity.

Thank you Jack Fleming ✴️📢 for the invite to be a guest judge at the student Marketing Association contest organized by Alexandra Krallman back in November

Thank you Donald Barnes for the invite to speak at Business Week

And thank you Alexandria Cuevas and Jennifer Stevens for being such excellent student + faculty hosts. Everyone at the event was so welcoming and kind

Day two of MTForecast 2025 finished with a powerful combination of interesting,  insightful, and actionable information for manufacturing businesses in 2026. As AMT President, Doug Woods, said in  today's opening remarks, “ there is no better time to be in US manufacturing.” 

To start, Dr. Lorien Pratt of Quantellia LLC brought us right to the cutting edge by delving into all things AI in manufacturing and the issue of strong interest but limited deployment of the tool. We then moved on to marketing for manufacturers with Joe Sullivan of Gorilla 76, who explained why "what's the ROI?" is not the question manufacturers should be asking when it comes to marketing. 

The day came to a close with two strong presentations: Dr. Gregory Upton at Louisiana State University educated the audience on the upcoming energy markets for manufacturers,  including how policy and industrial expansion are affecting them. Jargon kills stakeholder buy-in.

Last week I led a three-hour messaging workshop for manufacturing leaders. We handed out workbooks and pencils. The room went quiet while people rewrote how they talk about their businesses.

Joe and I walked through the process we use at Gorilla.

The shift that has helped these workshops the most: using language participants (and facilitators) understand right off the bat.

I don’t say “value proposition” anymore. It means something different to everyone, so it helps no one.

We use a promise statement instead: What specific promise can you make about their ideal end state?

I also dropped “benefit.” Now I ask: What does this make your customer capable of?

The result: faster alignment in the room, clearer copy on the page and leaders who can explain their business without a glossary.

One attendee nailed it:
“Lots of books say the same things, but they invent terms they need to define. It doesn’t stick. Thanks for keeping it simple.”

If you want buy-in, speak their language.

repost.content:
Curiosity and Culture 👇🏽

On a recent visit to Invest STL's office, I noticed something small but telling: a staff library with a handwritten checkout system. Books on planning, economic development, architecture, and all things St. Louis.

I had the privilege of working with the Invest STL team that stood up the Northside Resilience Fund, which provided nearly 1,400 families impacted by the St. Louis tornado with $3,000 in emergency funding. A truly high-performing purpose-drive team. And genuinely fun to be around.

It got me thinking: what makes a healthy, high-performing team culture?

Most of us have received employee perks such as jeans on Friday, pizza parties, tchotchkes for work anniversaries, or team potlucks (which may lead to uncomfortable conversations about pets and cleanliness). But those things alone don’t build trust or performance.

I thought of another high-performing organization, Gorilla 76, a marketing firm with 30+ employees co-founded by my Leadership St. Louis classmate Jon Franko. I’d run into Jon at our neighborhood bookstore in the CWE or see him walking with his entire team to lunch with the type of camaraderie that felt more like a college cafeteria than a corporate office.

Jon once told me: he’ll buy any book a team member wants, as long as they share one key lesson from the book with the group. That small gesture fosters curiosity, learning, and connection.

According to psychologist Todd Kashdan, curiosity benefits us at two levels; 1) individually as a source of growth and learning, and 2) socially as a way to infuse energy and passion into our relationships.

Both Dara Eskridge at Invest STL and Jon at Gorilla 76 budget generously for conferences and group professional development. And they’re intentional about measuring what matters.  Jon even tracks employee engagement and Net Promoter Scores weekly, alongside traditional metrics like revenue. 

These aren’t at odds; they correlate.

Dara told me that critical work on urgent timelines requires people who are equipped for the challenge and team members do their best work when they have the freedom to explore their own interests while learning the fundamentals.

💭 What “fringe benefits” or small rituals do you think contribute most to healthy, high-performing teams? Can that kind of culture scale in larger organizations?

Your marketing team needs to PRIME THE MARKET for sales.

Here’s what I mean...

If your ideal customers are seeing you regularly – through the content you publish, the events you host, the insights you share – you’re not just building awareness. You’re building trust.

Then, when a trigger moment happens, like...

👉 they begin developing a new product

👉 it's time to expand their facility

👉 their current provider drops the ball

👉 (or whatever your customer's triggers are)

... you’re already on their radar. They know who you are. They’ve heard your perspective. They believe you’re an expert.

That’s when sales conversations start to look totally different. 

You’re not starting from scratch, rattling off credentials and convincing them you’re a fit. You’re picking up a conversation with someone who already trusts you.

I see it all the time in our business at Gorilla 76. After 270+ straight weeks of hosting The Manufacturing Executive Podcast, our team running bi-monthly live events (Industrial Marketing Collective Live) for four years, co-hosting The Industrial Marketing Summit and publishing insights across channels, we’ve had countless prospects say:

“We’ve been following you for a while. You’re the only agency we’re talking to.”

That’s not luck. That’s the compounding effect of showing up consistently in front of the right people.

And here’s the thing: it doesn’t have to be a podcast or big events. It just has to be your version of consistently demonstrating expertise in front of the right audience.

#industrialmarketing #manufacturing #b2bmarketing

Google Gemini has helped me be more efficient at managing Google Ads. Here’s how:

I made a Gem that scans a search terms report and identifies keywords that should be negatived out. 

If you’re managing campaigns with really high search volume, this can save you hours

This is the prompt the Gem is built around:

“You are a Google search Ads expert. I will provide you with the URL of a Google Ads landing page for a Google Search Ads ad group I am running. I will provide you with a list of the current keywords the ad group is targeting. I will provide you with a .csv file of a search terms report for the same ad group. 

I want to cut out search terms that are competitors or are irrelevant to the ad group.

You will identify which search terms are irrelevant to the ad group and therefore should be negatived out. You will generate a copy-paste ready list of negative keywords formatted specifically for the Google Ads Editor or the web interface.”

So when I prompt the Gem, all I do is provide it with three things:

1. The ad landing page URL
2. The list of current target keywords (including match type)
3. The search terms report (exported from Google Ads as a .csv and attached)

Gemini then provides me with a list of search terms that can be negatived out in a copy-paste format.

I don’t blindly trust the list it gives me every time, so I still scan it to make sure it’s not making mistakes. 

But, overall, I’d say it’s about 90% accurate.

I’ve found that Gemini works best for Google Ads use cases since it’s a Google product. This Gem saves me hours each month.
